questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Constant from a Formula as resource types in Flow Builder?
options: A Constant holds a fixed value set once; a Formula calculates its value from other resources and recalculates automatically when those change
A Formula holds a fixed value set once; a Constant calculates its value from other resources and recalculates automatically when those change
Both Constant and Formula recalculate automatically whenever the flow runs; the only difference is their data type
A Constant can only hold numeric values, while a Formula can hold any data type
A Formula is only used inside Decision elements, never referenced elsewhere in a flow
A Constant and a Formula are two names for the same resource type; Flow Builder just displays them differently depending on context
questions.explain: A Constant is a value that never changes once you set it — a tax rate, a fixed threshold. A Formula is a value calculated from other resources, and Flow Builder recalculates it automatically whenever those underlying resources change. The two solve opposite problems: fixed-and-reused versus derived-and-recalculated.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the exact same two behaviors, just with the labels swapped — it claims Formula is the fixed one and Constant is the one that recalculates, which is backwards. Getting Constant and Formula's roles reversed is exactly the mistake this lesson's 'choosing the right one' guidance is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Flow Builder's two canvas layout styles are Auto-Layout and ________, with Auto-Layout being the one this course uses and the one Salesforce itself recommends for new flows.
questions.explain: Free-Form gives manual control over element placement and connectors, while Auto-Layout arranges and connects elements automatically and unlocks extra features like keyboard navigation and path highlighting — which is why Salesforce now recommends it, and why this course uses it throughout.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the Flow Builder screen (or canvas setting) to what it actually is.
right: The working area where elements are added and connected into a visual flow diagram
The top bar showing flow status plus controls like Save, Run, Debug, and Activate
The panel listing a flow's elements and resources, with the New Resource button
The recommended canvas style that arranges and connects elements automatically
questions.explain: The Toolbox lists a flow's elements and resources and has the New Resource button. The Canvas is the working area where elements get added and connected. The Button bar sits on top with flow status and controls like Save, Run, Debug, and Activate. Auto-Layout is the canvas style that handles arranging and connecting automatically.

questions.prompt: A Get Records element retrieves a record and automatically creates a variable to hold it, without you building one by hand first. What data type is that auto-created variable, and why does it matter for later elements in the flow?
options: It's a Record variable, holding every field from that record together — so a downstream element can reference any of its fields without a separate lookup
It's a Text variable holding only the record's Id — any other field needs a second Get Records call
It's a Boolean variable indicating whether a matching record was found, with no field data at all
It's a collection variable even when only one record matches, since Get Records always returns a list
questions.explain: A Record variable holds every field value from one Salesforce record at once, each still in its own data type. That's exactly what a Get Records element auto-generates when it finds a record, which is why downstream elements can reference any field on it directly instead of looking it up again.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about elements, connectors, and resources in Flow Builder, per Lesson 3.
options: Logic elements like Decision and Loop only affect data inside the running flow — a Data element or Action is still needed to make a change stick after the flow finishes
A resource appears as its own node on the canvas, the same way an element does
Connectors are the lines on the canvas that define which element the flow executes next
Interaction elements (Screen, Action, Subflow) are grouped by what they interact with — in this case, a user or another flow
Every element a flow uses must be built as a resource first, from the Toolbox's New Resource button
questions.explain: Logic elements only manipulate in-memory flow data, so a Data element or Action is still required to persist anything. Connectors are exactly the lines defining execution order. Interaction elements (Screen, Action, Subflow) are grouped because they all talk to a user or another flow. Resources, unlike elements, never appear as nodes on the canvas — elements reference them instead. And many elements, like Get Records, create their own resources automatically, so building one by hand first is not a requirement.

questions.prompt: A record-triggered flow is configured with "Optimize the Flow For" set to Fast Field Updates. It needs to create a related Task record when the trigger fires. What happens?
options: It can't — Fast Field Updates (before-save) can only update fields on the record that triggered the flow; creating any new record requires switching to Actions and Related Records (after-save)
It works exactly as configured — Fast Field Updates can create related records as long as the object is specified correctly
It creates the Task, but only after the triggering record's save completes, adding a second save automatically
It silently skips the Create Records element and continues, without any error
questions.explain: A before-save flow (Fast Field Updates) cannot create new records, update any record other than the one that triggered it, or run an Action. Creating a related Task requires the after-save option, Actions and Related Records, which runs once the triggering record is already saved.

questions.prompt: A flow's Start element subscribes to a platform event directly, versus a different flow that uses a Pause element to wait for a platform event mid-run. What's the actual distinction, per Lesson 12?
options: A Platform Event-Triggered Flow is born entirely from an incoming event message; a Pause element lets any already-running flow stop partway through and wait for one before continuing
They're the same mechanism — Pause is just an older name for a Platform Event-Triggered Flow's Start element
Only a Pause element can filter which event messages count; a Platform Event-Triggered Flow's Start element reacts to every message on the event regardless of field values
A Platform Event-Triggered Flow requires a screen, while a Pause element never does
questions.explain: A Platform Event-Triggered Flow's Start element subscribes to an event and the flow launches fresh each time a message arrives. A Pause element is a different mechanism entirely: any autolaunched flow that's already running can pause mid-flow and wait for a platform event message, with its own filter conditions, before resuming.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on a record-triggered flow's Configure Start panel, choosing "Actions and Related Records" instead of Fast Field Updates means the flow runs ________ the triggering record is saved to the database.
questions.explain: Actions and Related Records is the after-save option — the flow runs once the triggering record is already saved, which is exactly what unlocks updating other records, creating new records, and running Actions.

questions.prompt: Match each flow type covered in Chapter 2 to what actually starts it.
right: A user action — a button, quick action, tab, or link
A message published onto Salesforce's event bus
A specified date, time, and frequency, run in the background
Apex, another flow, a REST API call, or a button/link URL — nothing built-in
questions.explain: A Schedule-Triggered Flow runs at a set date, time, and frequency. A Screen Flow is launched by a user clicking something. A Platform Event-Triggered Flow launches when a subscribed event message arrives. Autolaunched Flow (No Trigger) has no built-in starter at all — it needs Apex, another flow, a REST API call, or a button/link to invoke it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Subflow elements and the flows they call, per Lesson 11.
options: A child flow's variable must have "Available for input" checked before a parent's Set Input Values section can populate it
A Subflow element can call any flow type, including another screen flow or a record-triggered flow directly as the referenced flow
The parent flow waits for the referenced flow to finish before continuing past the Subflow element
Reusing the same referenced flow from three different parent flows means fixing a shared piece of logic in one place instead of three
Available for input and Available for output are flow-level settings, not settings on an individual variable
questions.explain: A child flow's variable must explicitly opt in via Available for input before a parent's Set Input Values can populate it, and the parent flow does wait for the referenced flow to finish. Reuse across multiple parent flows is the whole point — one place to fix shared logic. Subflow calls an already-built autolaunched flow, not any arbitrary flow type like a screen or record-triggered flow. And Available for input/output are per-variable settings inside the child flow, not flow-level settings.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of configuring and using a Subflow element in the correct order, per Lesson 11.
items: In the child flow, create a variable and check "Available for input" under Availability Outside the Flow
In the parent flow, add a Subflow element and set its Referenced Flow to the child flow
In the Subflow element's Set Input Values section, map a parent-flow value into the child flow's input variable
The parent flow pauses at the Subflow element while the referenced flow runs to completion
questions.explain: The child flow's variable has to be exposed for input before anything can be mapped into it. Only then does the parent's Subflow element reference that child flow, map a value into the now-exposed input variable, and finally hand off control — pausing until the referenced flow finishes before the parent continues.

questions.prompt: Per the Loops lesson, what is the single most important rule to follow when building a Loop element in Flow Builder?
options: Keep Get Records before the loop, and keep Create, Update, and Delete Records after the loop, rather than placing any of them inside the loop's For Each path
Always include a Get Records element inside the loop so each iteration has fresh data
Never use an Assignment element inside a loop, since Assignment can only run outside one
Limit every loop to exactly 50 iterations regardless of collection size
Place the Update Records element inside the loop, but move the Get Records element before it
Loops should never contain more than one element on the For Each path
questions.explain: Get Records, Create Records, Update Records, and Delete Records each run a real SOQL query or DML operation, and a flow is limited to 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML operations per transaction. Keeping Get Records before the loop and the write elements after it means those operations run once against the whole collection, instead of once per item, no matter how large the batch is.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E gets the Get Records placement right but still puts Update Records — a DML element — inside the loop. That still means one DML operation fires per iteration, which can still blow past the 150-DML-statement ceiling on a large collection. Fixing only one of the two element placements isn't the rule the lesson teaches; both reads and writes have to move outside the loop.

questions.prompt: You have a 50-record Opportunity collection. You run a Collection Sort element configured to sort it by Amount descending and keep only the top 10, selecting that same collection variable as the one to sort. Afterward, how many records does that original collection variable hold, and why?
options: 10 — Collection Sort modifies the very collection variable you select, in place, and its truncation setting discards everything past the limit
50 — Collection Sort always writes its result to a brand-new variable, leaving the one you selected untouched
60 — Collection Sort appends the sorted top 10 onto the existing 50 without removing anything
0 — selecting a collection variable as both the input and output of a Collection Sort empties it
questions.explain: Unlike Collection Filter, which creates a new collection and leaves the original untouched, Collection Sort modifies the collection you select in place — and because it can also truncate, keeping only the top 10 after sorting discards the other 40 records from that same variable.

questions.prompt: A flow needs to set every record in a 150-record collection's Status field to the same literal value, "Closed," and copy each record's Id unchanged. Per Lesson 19, why is a Transform element Salesforce's recommended approach here instead of a Loop with an Assignment inside it?
options: Transform elements run roughly 10 times faster than loops doing the same task and scale better, reducing the chance of hitting the flow's execution time limit
A Loop element cannot set a field to the same literal value for every record — only Transform supports a static Value
Transform is required because Assignment elements cannot reference a collection variable at all
Loops are being deprecated and will stop working in a future release
questions.explain: Salesforce's own guidance is that Transform elements run roughly 10 times faster than an equivalent loop and scale better as flows get more complex — which is why the rule of thumb is to use Transform whenever a task can be expressed that way, reserving Loop for cases like calling an Action per item that Transform genuinely can't do.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Create Records, Update Records, and Delete Records elements, per Lesson 17.
options: On a before-save record-triggered flow, Update Records can only use "the record that triggered the flow" as its How to Find Records method — the other three methods require after-save
Create Records can set field values either manually or from a record variable that already holds the values
Delete Records deserves more caution than Create or Update, and should be reserved for records that genuinely should never have existed
Update Records can only find records to update by filtering on conditions — it cannot use the triggering record directly
All three elements require a screen so the user can confirm the operation before it runs
questions.explain: A before-save flow can only update the triggering record itself — the other three How to Find Records methods need after-save. Create Records lets you set values manually or from an existing record variable. Delete Records is explicitly called out as needing the most caution of the three, reserved for records that should never have existed. Update Records can absolutely use the triggering record directly — that's actually its first and simplest method. None of these elements require a screen; all three run without user interaction.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Decision element performs the equivalent of an ________ statement, evaluating a set of conditions and routing the flow down the matching outcome's path.
questions.explain: Salesforce's own description of the Decision element calls it the equivalent of an if-then statement: it evaluates conditions and routes execution down whichever outcome's conditions are met, falling through to the Default Outcome if none are.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 3 element to what it actually does.
right: Changes a variable's value in memory only, with no effect on Salesforce until a data element saves it
Reshapes a whole collection at once by mapping source fields to target fields, with no per-item path to build
Removes non-matching values into a new collection, leaving the original untouched
Reorders a collection's values in place, optionally truncating it to a set number of records
questions.explain: Collection Filter creates a new, narrowed collection and leaves the original alone. Collection Sort reorders the same collection in place and can truncate it. Transform reshapes an entire collection via field mappings, with no loop body to build. Assignment only changes a variable's in-memory value — it never saves anything on its own.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the bulkified "deactivate inactive users" pattern from the Loops lesson in the correct order.
items: Get Active Users (Get Records) runs once, before the loop, retrieving the whole collection to check
UserLoop iterates the collection; a Decision checks each user's days since last login
An Assignment element inside the loop sets the current item's Active field to false in memory only, for users past the threshold
After the loop's After Last path, a single Update Records element commits every changed user in one DML operation
questions.explain: Get Records runs once before the loop to retrieve every candidate user. Inside the loop, a Decision checks each user's inactivity, and an Assignment element flips the in-memory Active value for the ones that qualify — without touching the database. Only after the loop finishes does a single Update Records element commit every change in one DML operation, exactly the bulkification pattern the lesson warns you to follow.

questions.prompt: A Create Records element has no fault path attached, and the create fails because a required field is blank. Per Lesson 20, what does the user running the flow actually see?
options: A generic, unhelpful error — an unhandled fault — rather than the real system error text
The literal $Flow.FaultMessage text, since Flow Builder always surfaces it by default even with no fault path
Nothing — the flow silently completes as if the create had succeeded
A prompt asking them to manually fill in the missing required field before continuing
questions.explain: Without a fault path, a failed element throws an unhandled fault and the user sees a generic, unhelpful error rather than the real system message. Attaching a fault path with $Flow.FaultMessage is what surfaces the actual error text instead.

questions.prompt: A flow passes Debug when run as yourself, a System Administrator, but a lower-access user reports it fails for them in production. Per Lesson 21, what debug option reproduces their experience, and why might running it as yourself have missed the problem?
options: Run automation as another user — a System Administrator's debug run has no sharing or field-level-access restrictions, so it can't surface a failure caused by the real user's more limited access
Run automation in rollback mode — it specifically simulates a lower-access user's permissions
Flow Test — Debug and Flow Test are the same feature under different names, so either would reproduce it equally
There's no way to reproduce another user's exact experience short of logging in as them directly
questions.explain: Run automation as another user lets you debug exactly as a specific, lower-access user would experience the flow. Debugging as yourself — almost always a System Administrator with no sharing restrictions — can hide access-related failures that only show up for a more restricted real user.

questions.code:
Loop over Opportunities in collection
  Get Records: find the related Account
  Update Records: update that one Account
End Loop
questions.prompt: This pattern runs against a 200-record batch of Opportunities. Select every true statement about what happens, per Lessons 22-23.
options: It issues 200 separate Get Records calls and 200 separate Update Records calls, one pair per Opportunity
It can hit the 100-SOQL-queries-per-transaction and 150-DML-statements-per-transaction ceilings, since Flow shares governor limits with Apex
This pattern is safe because Flow has its own separate, higher governor limits than Apex
Moving the Get Records and Update Records elements outside the loop — querying and updating the whole Account collection once — fixes the problem without changing the outcome
The fix requires rewriting the logic in Apex, since Flow cannot be restructured to avoid this pattern
questions.explain: With a query and a DML element both inside the loop, 200 Opportunities produce 200 separate SOQL queries and 200 separate DML statements — real operations that can exceed the 100-query and 150-statement ceilings Flow shares with Apex in the same transaction. Flow does not get its own separate limits. The fix is exactly the bulkification pattern from Lesson 22: collect the Account Ids inside the loop, then query and update the whole collection once, outside it — no Apex rewrite required.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: activating a new version of a flow automatically ________ whichever version was active before, so a flow never ends up with two active versions running at once.
questions.explain: Only one version of a flow can be active at any time. Activating a new version automatically deactivates the previously active one, which is also exactly why rolling back to a known-good version is as simple as reactivating it from the Versions list.

questions.prompt: Match each Flow Orchestration term to what it actually is, per Lesson 25.
right: Runs an autolaunched flow with no human interaction required
A named grouping of related steps; only one in progress per record at a time
The overall structure coordinating a multi-stage, multi-person business process
Runs a screen flow and shows up as a work item a person has to open and complete
questions.explain: An orchestration is the overall structure coordinating a multi-stage process. A stage is a named grouping of steps, with only one in progress per record at a time. An interactive step runs a screen flow as a work item someone has to complete. A background step runs an autolaunched flow with no human interaction at all.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of safely deploying a new flow version, per Lesson 24, in the correct order.
items: Build and test the new version, often starting in a sandbox
Confirm it behaves correctly using Debug and a saved Flow Test
Activate that specific version in the target org
If a problem surfaces later, reactivate the last known-good version from the Versions list instead of rebuilding it
questions.explain: A new version is built and tested first, then verified with Debug and a saved Flow Test before it's ever activated for real users. Activation is the deliberate, final step. Because old versions stay around deactivated rather than disappearing, recovering from a bad deployment is just reactivating the last known-good version, not reconstructing it from memory.

questions.prompt: An org has six separate After-Save record-triggered flows on the Opportunity object, each checking a different field. Per Lesson 26, what's the recommended fix?
options: Consolidate them into one Opportunity, After-Save flow, using Decision elements to branch into the logic that used to live in each separate flow
Leave them as six separate flows, since Salesforce guarantees a predictable execution order across any number of flows on the same object and context
Convert all six into Scheduled Flows so they no longer compete for the same trigger context
Delete five of the six and keep only the oldest one active
questions.explain: Salesforce's own recommendation is one flow per object per trigger context. Six scattered After-Save flows on Opportunity should become one flow, with Decision elements branching into whatever logic each separate flow used to handle — same business rules, one place to read and debug, one predictable order.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about naming and documenting flows, per Lesson 27.
options: A workable flow-naming pattern is Object – Trigger Context – Purpose
An element labeled "Decision" or "Get Records 2" tells a future reader nothing about why it exists, even though the flow itself still runs correctly
The flow's Description field is optional on any flow expected to still be running in six months
A self-documenting canvas with clear element labels can often be understood top to bottom without opening a single element's configuration
Clear element labels require more configuration effort than vague default ones, which is why vague names are common in practice
questions.explain: Object – Trigger Context – Purpose is exactly the naming pattern the lesson recommends. A vaguely labeled element still functions, but tells a future reader nothing about intent, while clear labels turn the canvas itself into documentation that's readable top to bottom. The Description field is explicitly not optional except on a throwaway test — and clear labels cost nothing extra to type, so effort isn't what makes vague names common.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Migrate to Flow tool, per Lesson 28.
options: It converts workflow rules and processes one at a time — a single workflow rule becomes a single new flow
A workflow rule that only updates fields becomes a before-save flow, since those actions don't need an after-save context
The newly created flow starts out active immediately, replacing the old workflow rule the moment migration runs
Running the tool on eight old workflow rules on the same object, without further work, recreates the same automation-sprawl problem as eight separate flows
After migration, the original workflow rule is deleted automatically so there's no chance of both running at once
questions.explain: Migrate to Flow is a deliberate 1-to-1 tool: one workflow rule becomes one new flow, and a field-update-only rule becomes a faster before-save flow. Migrating eight rules at once still produces eight separate flows — the exact automation sprawl Lesson 26 warns against, unless you consolidate afterward. The new flow actually starts out inactive, not active, and the original workflow rule stays active until you deliberately use the one-click switch activations action — it is never deleted automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: as of December 31, 2025, Salesforce no longer ________ Workflow Rules and Process Builder — meaning no further bug fixes or new features, even though existing active automation keeps running.
questions.explain: End of support is not a shutdown: Salesforce stopped maintaining Workflow Rules and Process Builder as of December 31, 2025, but existing active rules and processes continue to run exactly as before. The message is to migrate on your own timeline, not that anything breaks on that date.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Lead Assignment practice lab, the fault path off Get Territory Rule writes {!$Flow.FaultMessage} onto a field on the Lead record itself, instead of showing a Display Text screen, because the flow runs ________ — a trigger context where screen elements can't be used at all.
questions.explain: Before-save and autolaunched flows can't use screen elements. The Lead Assignment lab's flow runs before-save, so its fault path has nowhere to display a screen — writing $Flow.FaultMessage onto a field on the record itself is the only way to surface the real error to an admin.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Case Escalation practice lab's bulkified notification pattern in the correct order.
items: A Scheduled Path fires 4 hours after the Case's CreatedDate and checks whether the case is still open and unescalated
Get Case Team Members (Get Records) retrieves every CaseTeamMember record for the case, as a collection
A loop adds each team member's email to a single emailCollection variable, without sending anything itself
One Send Email action, outside the loop, sends to the whole emailCollection at once
questions.explain: The Scheduled Path waits 4 hours and re-checks the case's status before doing anything else. Get Case Team Members then retrieves the whole team as one collection. The loop that follows only builds up emailCollection in memory — it never sends anything itself. Only after the loop finishes does a single Send Email action fire, addressed to the entire collection at once, exactly the bulkified pattern that avoids one email send per team member.
